title: Anaphylaxis
banner: DRAFT, NOT clinically reviewed. Fictional scenario specification; never imported, published or shown to learners.
learning_objectives: Recognise new airway or breathing involvement after a suspected trigger and immediately activate the anaphylaxis pathway with first-line IM adrenaline under the authorised emergency protocol.
Know the injection site named on the epinephrine label for anaphylaxis.
Understand that medicine choice and doses are prescriber or protocol decisions.
Monitor closely and report the reaction afterwards.

sources.use: FDA epinephrine label: injection site and extravasation statements
RCUK anaphylaxis guideline 2021: key recommendations and sections on setting, monitoring, positioning and removing the trigger

required_sources: Anaphylaxis guideline text sections not read (refractory anaphylaxis, observation after treatment, fluids)
Unit anaphylaxis protocol and the adverse reaction reporting route
Local 2025 ERC/RCUK crosswalk and anaphylaxis monitoring/observation protocol, including refractory escalation scope for ICU staff
gaps: No published clinical scenario may exist until the review phase: this is a specification only.
The branching content, consequences and scoring are the author's reading of the cited sources and have had no clinical review.
Refractory anaphylaxis, fluids, airway steps and observation duration were not read and are not written; the RCUK guideline is copyright and is paraphrased only.
Doses and routes other than the label's injection-site statement are deliberately absent.

The Resuscitation Council UK healthcare-provider anaphylaxis guidance remains May 2021; 2025 first-aid / ERC special-circumstances statements are contextual and do not alone replace the in-hospital authorised emergency protocol. Full refractory management remains specialist-led.
permissions: Cited sources are paraphrased only; see the licensing register for each source's reproduction status.
RCUK guideline: no reproduction without written permission.
setting: A fictional adult receiving an intravenous antibiotic on a fictional unit.

steps.info: Ten minutes after an antibiotic infusion starts, the patient reports itching and feels short of breath and the face looks swollen.

options.text: Immediately stop the suspected antibiotic trigger, call for emergency help, assess ABCDE and give or request prompt IM adrenaline under the authorised anaphylaxis emergency protocol without awaiting routine ward-round orders. Position safely for the patient's airway and circulation; avoid standing or sudden walking.
options.feedback: Suspected anaphylaxis with airway, breathing or circulatory involvement is time-critical; prompt IM adrenaline and clinical resuscitation are prioritized in RCUK healthcare-provider guidance. The drug and administration are governed by a trained clinician and institution's authorised emergency pathway; never treat an antihistamine as the first-line substitute.
options.consequence: Emergency assistance is activated and protocol-authorised first-line treatment is promptly arranged while the suspected trigger is stopped.

options.text: Slow the infusion and see whether the symptoms settle.
options.feedback: Continuing a drug during a suspected serious reaction is unsafe.
options.consequence: The swelling and breathing difficulty worsen.

options.text: Give an antihistamine from the ward stock and continue the infusion.
options.feedback: Medicines need an order, and the infusion should be stopped first.
options.consequence: The reaction progresses while time is lost.

steps.info: The emergency anaphylaxis pathway has been activated and trained staff are preparing or administering the authorised first-line IM adrenaline. The team asks you to confirm the labelled injection-site principle.
steps.prompt: Where does the label say it should be injected?

options.text: In the anterolateral thigh, avoiding the buttocks, digits, hands and feet.
options.feedback: For the labelled IM anaphylaxis use, the anterolateral thigh is the specified site. This is a knowledge check for the team, **not a reason to delay a time-critical prescribed or protocol-authorised first dose**.
options.consequence: The injection is given at the correct site and the team continues treatment.

options.text: In the deltoid, because the arm is quicker to reach.
options.feedback: The label says injection into smaller muscles such as the deltoid is not recommended.
options.consequence: The injection is given but at a less suitable site.

options.text: In the buttock, because the muscle is large.
options.feedback: The label says not to inject into the buttocks.
options.consequence: The injection is given at a site the label advises against.

steps.info: The patient is improving and the team is deciding what happens next.

options.text: Continue trained close monitoring for recurrent airway, breathing or circulatory problems, ensure observation and positioning follow the emergency team's plan, document the suspected trigger and treatments, and support handover and allergy follow-up.
options.feedback: Initial improvement does not eliminate the risk of recurrence or continued deterioration. The emergency team determines observation duration and discharge planning; documenting and flagging the suspect antibiotic helps prevent future inadvertent exposure.
options.consequence: The reaction is recorded as an allergy, the team plans the next steps and the referral is made.

options.text: Transfer the patient to the ward without monitoring because the symptoms have settled.
options.feedback: Symptoms can return and monitoring must continue as the team directs.
options.consequence: The patient deteriorates again on the ward without monitoring.

options.text: Restart the antibiotic at a slower speed once the symptoms have gone.
options.feedback: Restarting a suspected trigger is a prescriber decision.

learning_points: New breathing/airway compromise after an antibiotic may be anaphylaxis: stop the suspected trigger, activate emergency help and ensure timely protocol-authorised IM adrenaline.
The epinephrine label names the anterolateral thigh for injection in anaphylaxis.
Medicine choices and restarting a drug are prescriber decisions.
Monitor, document and report the reaction.
Do not delay anaphylaxis first-line emergency treatment to answer an injection-site knowledge question or wait for a non-urgent prescription workflow.
